page.title: OpenAI’s mathematics release
page.description: Read OpenAI’s papers, compare their theorems with statements written in Lean, and see what independent groups reported when they examined the statements or ran proof-verification programs.
page.redirect_text: The map of the release is now the front page.
page.independent: An independent guide to OpenAI’s papers, not affiliated with OpenAI.
page.nojs: The interactive map needs JavaScript. The list below links to every group of related papers. The Agent navigation link opens instructions for reading the map as JSON.

release.s1: OpenAI published {manuscripts_current} current papers across {disciplines} disciplines. It groups related papers into {families} “families”.
release.s2: {families_with_lean} families have statements written in Lean, a language for mathematical statements and proofs that a computer can verify. There are {statements_lean} such statement files.
release.s3: OpenAI labels {statements_lean_main_results} of the {statements_lean} Lean statement files as main results in its Lean catalogue.
release.s4: The papers cite one another in {internal_citation_edges} directed pairs and cite {external_works_cited} works outside the release. OpenAI has withdrawn {manuscripts_withdrawn} papers and replaced {manuscripts_previous_editions} with later editions.
release.s5: Atlas links public contributions credited to {community_people} names and places {community_findings} reports beside the results they discuss.

since.heading: Since the release.
since.text: OpenAI has withdrawn {withdrawn}: {papers}. It has replaced {editions} with later editions.

key.heading: What the colours mean
key.intro: The colours compare two groups’ assessments of the Lean statements: do those statements express the result OpenAI describes in its catalogue?
key.all: Both groups find the whole result stated or implied
key.part: Only part of the result, or a narrower statement
key.other: A supporting step or a different result
key.split: The groups disagree about what the Lean statements express
key.none: No Lean statement in the release
key.unread: No comparison recorded from either group
key.size: A disc’s area grows with the number of paper results and Lean statements it shows.
key.citations: Inside a discipline, pointing at a family draws its citations to the families beside it: brick where its papers cite, grey where they are cited.
key.readers: The groups are MathVet and Carlos Toledo’s cert-machine. Open a family page to read each group’s assessment and method. These colours do not say whether a paper’s proof is correct.
key.count_link: {n} families: show them on the Families list
key.counted: These counts are groups of related papers. {numbers} also counts the release’s {files} individually and lists an AI agent’s {drafts}. Those unreviewed drafts do not determine the colours.

items.name: Erdős’s reciprocal-sum conjecture
items.why: Erdős conjectured that a set of positive integers whose reciprocals add up to infinity contains arithmetic progressions of every length. The family’s one paper claims a proof.

items.name: The quasi-Riemann hypothesis
items.why: OpenAI’s catalogue describes a proof that no Dirichlet L-function, the Riemann zeta function included, has a zero with real part greater than 7/8.

items.name: The spacetime Penrose inequality
items.why: Penrose’s inequality bounds the mass of a spacetime from below by the smallest area enclosing its black holes. OpenAI’s catalogue describes a proof, under stated hypotheses, in every spatial dimension from three up.

items.name: Borsuk’s conjecture in dimension nine
items.why: Borsuk asked whether every bounded set in n dimensions splits into n + 1 pieces of smaller diameter. The paper constructs a set in dimension nine that does not.

bands.index_intro: Each family is a group of related papers in OpenAI’s catalogue. Open its page to read those papers and the reports about them.
bands.checked_heading: Who examined the release, and how
bands.checked_intro: These groups report different kinds of work: verifying a formal proof with a program, comparing a Lean statement with a paper, or testing a finite claim by calculation. Atlas links their original reports and has not repeated their work.
bands.checked_cert: ran Comparator on OpenAI’s proofs with a second independent verifier, tested finite claims in some papers by exact calculation, and compared the Lean statements with OpenAI’s catalogue descriptions.
bands.checked_mathvet: ran Comparator on OpenAI’s proofs in an isolated environment and compared the Lean statements with OpenAI’s catalogue descriptions under published assessment rules.
bands.checked_neal: ran Comparator on OpenAI’s proofs using Lean’s own proof verifier and recorded the time and memory used.
bands.checked_hol: proved selected intermediate steps using HOL Light, a different proof assistant, and tested incorrect examples that the program should reject.
bands.checked_erdos: identifies which Erdős problems the papers address. These links do not assess whether the claimed proofs are correct.
bands.checked_more_link: Every source, with what each one reports
bands.help_intro: Each contribution covers one result or one page, and is credited by name on the pages it changes.
bands.help_without: Open a short GitHub form to explain a result, compare a Lean statement with its paper, or report a problem with a page.
bands.help_with: Give your assistant the start-here guide from the repository. It helps you choose one useful note, drafts it privately and leaves the signing to you.
bands.help_queue: Some Lean statements have a specific reason to be read first.
